situation: Two people are introduced at a social event.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Hi, I'm John. Nice to meet you.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Nice to meet you too. I'm Aditi.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Where are you from, Aditi?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: I'm from Mumbai, but I've been in London for two years.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: How do you like it?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: I love it, apart from the winters.

keyExpressions: Nice to meet you. — Nice to meet you too.
I've been here for two years.
remember: 'Nice to meet you' is only for a first meeting. When you see the person again, say 'good to see you'.

situation: Two friends try to find a time to meet.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Are you free this weekend?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Saturday I'm busy, but Sunday's open. What did you have in mind?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: There's a new place near the park. Fancy lunch?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Sounds great. What time?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Around one?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Perfect. See you there.

keyExpressions: What did you have in mind?
remember: 'Fancy…?' is a very common British way to suggest something informally. Americans would say 'Do you want to…?'.

situation: One friend has to cancel at short notice.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: I'm really sorry, but I'm going to have to cancel tonight.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Oh no, everything OK?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Work thing blew up and I'll be here till late. I feel terrible.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Don't worry about it, honestly. Another time.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Definitely. Can I make it up to you next week?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: You can buy me dinner.

keyExpressions: I'm going to have to cancel.
Can I make it up to you?
remember: Cancel, apologise, and immediately propose an alternative. Cancelling without offering a new date reads as a brush-off.

situation: You need help but do not want to interrupt someone who is busy.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Are you in the middle of something, or do you have two minutes?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: I've got a few minutes. What's up?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: I can't get the export to work and I've tried everything I know.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Show me what you've done so far.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Thanks — I really appreciate it.

keyExpressions: Are you in the middle of something?
remember: Asking about their availability first, before describing the problem, is what makes this polite.

situation: Two colleagues disagree about an approach without falling out.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: I think we should launch in June and fix issues as they come up.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: I see the appeal, but I'm not sure we'd recover from a bad first impression.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Fair. What would you need to feel comfortable?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Two more weeks of testing. That's all.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: That's not unreasonable. Let's put mid-June to the group.

keyExpressions: What would you need to feel comfortable?
remember: Acknowledge the other view before disagreeing. 'I see the appeal, but…' keeps the disagreement about the idea, not the person.

situation: You have made an error that affected someone else's work.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: I owe you an apology — I sent the old version to the client.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Ah. Have they opened it?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Not yet. I've already sent the correct one with a note.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Then it's fine. Thanks for telling me straight away.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: I've added a check to the process so it can't happen again.

keyExpressions: Thanks for telling me straight away.
remember: Apologise, say what you have already done to fix it, then say what will prevent a repeat. Explaining why it happened comes last, if at all.

situation: One person invites two friends; one accepts and one cannot come.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: We're having a few people over on Saturday — can you both make it?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: I'd love to. What time?

conversation.speaker: C
conversation.text: I'd love to as well, but we're away that weekend. Sorry.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: No problem — next time.

conversation.speaker: C
conversation.text: Definitely. Have a great evening.

remember: 'I'd love to, but…' is the standard polite refusal. Starting with 'no' sounds much colder than English speakers expect.

situation: Two colleagues share a lift for thirty seconds.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Morning.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Morning. Busy day?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Back-to-back meetings. You?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Quiet, thankfully.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Enjoy it while it lasts.

remember: Very short exchanges like this are normal and complete. You do not need to keep the conversation going.

situation: A manager gives a team member honest but supportive feedback.

conversation.speaker: Manager
conversation.text: The analysis was strong. I want to talk about the delivery, though.

conversation.speaker: Team member
conversation.text: Go on.

conversation.speaker: Manager
conversation.text: You covered everything, but the main finding didn't come out until slide fourteen.

conversation.speaker: Team member
conversation.text: That's fair. I was worried about jumping to conclusions.

conversation.speaker: Manager
conversation.text: Lead with the conclusion and use the rest to support it. Try that next time.

conversation.speaker: Team member
conversation.text: I will. Thanks — that's useful.

remember: Useful feedback names one specific behaviour and one specific change. General praise or criticism changes nothing.

situation: Calling someone back after missing them.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Hi, it's Sam — I saw you called earlier.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Thanks for getting back to me. It was about Thursday.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Right, is there a problem with the time?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: The room's double-booked. Could we do the morning instead?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Morning works. I'll update the invite.

keyExpressions: Thanks for getting back to me.
remember: Opening with your name is essential on the phone. The other person may not have your number saved.

situation: Someone asks you a question in a meeting that you cannot answer immediately.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: What's the cost impact of moving the date?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: That's a good question, and I'd rather give you an accurate number than a guess.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: How long do you need?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Give me until tomorrow afternoon and I'll have it broken down properly.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: That's fine.

keyExpressions: I'd rather give you an accurate number than a guess.
I'll come back to you with…
remember: Saying you will check is far stronger than guessing. Always attach a specific time to the promise.

situation: You are not sure you followed what someone said.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: So send it to Neha first, then to finance once she's signed it.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Sorry, just to check — Neha first, then finance?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: That's right.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: And if she's away?

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Then straight to finance and copy her in.

remember: Repeating instructions back in your own words is the fastest way to catch a misunderstanding — and it never sounds unintelligent.

situation: Thanking a colleague who went out of their way to help.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: I wanted to say thank you for staying late last night.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Oh, it was no trouble.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: It was, and it made a real difference — we'd have missed the deadline.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Well, in that case, you're welcome.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Let me get lunch tomorrow.

keyExpressions: I wanted to say thank you for…
remember: Naming the specific thing they did, and its effect, makes thanks feel genuine rather than automatic.

situation: A buyer and seller work towards a price they can both accept.

conversation.speaker: Buyer
conversation.text: The quote came in higher than we budgeted.

conversation.speaker: Seller
conversation.text: I understand. What figure did you have in mind?

conversation.speaker: Buyer
conversation.text: We were thinking around fifteen per cent lower.

conversation.speaker: Seller
conversation.text: I can't get to fifteen, but I could do eight if we extend to two years.

conversation.speaker: Buyer
conversation.text: Let me take that back to the team.

keyExpressions: That came in higher than we budgeted.
What figure did you have in mind?
I can't get to…, but I could do…
Let me take that back to the team.
remember: 'I can't do X, but I could do Y' keeps a negotiation alive. A flat 'no' usually ends it.

situation: A new starter is shown around by a colleague.

conversation.speaker: Colleague
conversation.text: Welcome! I'm Tom, I sit just over there.

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: Thanks. I'm Yusuf — today's my first day, so please be patient with me.

conversation.speaker: Colleague
conversation.text: Don't worry, everyone's been there. Have you got your laptop set up?

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: Not yet. Who should I ask about that?

conversation.speaker: Colleague
conversation.text: IT are on the second floor. I'll walk you up.

remember: 'Who should I ask about…?' is more useful than 'how do I…?' — in a new place, finding the right person matters more than the answer.

situation: Chasing a colleague for something they promised.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Quick one — is the budget sheet still on your list?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: It is, sorry. It got pushed by the audit.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: No problem. Is Thursday realistic, or should I tell them Monday?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Say Monday, and I'll try for Friday.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Perfect, that helps.

remember: Asking what is realistic, rather than repeating the original deadline, gets you an honest answer instead of a defensive one.

situation: Buying fruit at a market.

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: How much are the mangoes?

conversation.speaker: Seller
conversation.text: Three for five pounds, or two pounds each.

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: I'll take three, please. Are they ripe?

conversation.speaker: Seller
conversation.text: Ready today or tomorrow.

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: Perfect. Do you take card?

conversation.speaker: Seller
conversation.text: Card's fine.

remember: 'How much is…' for one item, 'how much are…' for several. It is a small slip that native speakers notice.

situation: The connection is bad during a video meeting.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Sorry, you're breaking up. Could you say that again?

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: Is that better? Let me turn my camera off.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Much better, thanks.

conversation.speaker: B
conversation.text: I was saying we should push the review to next week.

conversation.speaker: A
conversation.text: Got it. I'll send a new invite.

remember: 'You're breaking up' means the audio is cutting out — it is the standard phrase on any bad connection.
'I was saying…' is how you resume after an interruption.

situation: Resigning from a job you have enjoyed.

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: I've got something difficult to tell you. I've accepted another role.

conversation.speaker: Manager
conversation.text: I'm sorry to hear that, though I can't say I'm shocked. Congratulations.

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: Thank you. I've genuinely valued working here — this was a hard decision.

conversation.speaker: Manager
conversation.text: When would your last day be?

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: A month from Friday, and I'll make sure the handover is thorough.

keyExpressions: I've got something difficult to tell you.
I'll make sure the handover is thorough.
remember: Lead with the decision, not the reasons. Offering a clean handover is what people remember afterwards.

situation: Ordering a drink to take away.

conversation.speaker: Barista
conversation.text: What can I get you?

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: A large flat white, please.

conversation.speaker: Barista
conversation.text: To have in or take away?

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: Take away, thanks.

conversation.speaker: Barista
conversation.text: That's three fifty. Name for the cup?

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: Sam. S-A-M.

keyExpressions: To have in or take away?
remember: 'For here or to go?' is the American version of 'have in or take away?'. Both mean the same thing.

situation: Following up on a payment that is overdue.

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: I'm calling about invoice 3312 — it was due two weeks ago.

conversation.speaker: Them
conversation.text: Let me look… I don't see it as approved yet.

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: Is there anything you need from us to move it along?

conversation.speaker: Them
conversation.text: A purchase order number would help.

conversation.speaker: You
conversation.text: I'll send that over today. Could we aim for payment by the end of the week?

keyExpressions: It was due two weeks ago.
Is there anything you need from us?
remember: Asking what they need turns a complaint into a shared problem, which usually gets paid faster than pressure does.
